source.title_on_document: From Planning to Revision: How AI Writing Support at Different Stages Alters Ownership

supplement.where: No supplement is referenced. Appendices A to I (prompts, interface, LLM prompts, survey, quality control, grading, thematic codebook, model specifications, full results) are inside this PDF, pp. 18-32.
supplement.holds: Not applicable. Table 6 (p. 29) holds all adjusted means with 95% CIs; Table 8 (p. 32) holds the active-user robustness means.

paper_design_summary: Prolific participants (n = 253 analyzed) wrote a 200-300 word argumentative essay in three timed stages (outline, draft, revision) and were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: no AI, AI ideas and outlines for planning, an AI-generated draft from the participant's own outline, or AI revision suggestions. The paper's main outcomes are self-reported ownership and self-reported attribution of ideas and text to AI; the only outcome scored on the output is essay quality on an IELTS-based 0-9 rubric, graded by o4-mini calibrated on 50 essays graded by an English teacher.

studies.label: Online between-subjects experiment on stage of AI writing support (argumentative essay)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writing-stage condition: no AI, AI support for planning, AI-generated draft, or AI support for revision. Separately, participants were randomly assigned to one of two sets of essay topics and then chose one topic from that set.
assignment.quote: We designed our conditions to match typical AI support for writing in each stage. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions:
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3; topic-set randomization p. 3, Section 3.1; between-subjects design p. 3, Section 3
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is mentioned. The paper calls its exclusion criteria 'pre-specified' (p. 5, Section 3.4) and its contrasts C1-C3 'pre-specified' (p. 7, Section 4.4).

arms.name: no ai
arms.description: No AI support; participant writes outline, draft, and revision alone.

arms.name: ai plan
arms.description: During planning only, participant can request AI thesis statements (three at first, then one at a time) and full outlines for a generated thesis; can copy and paste them. Drafts and revises alone.

arms.name: ai draft
arms.description: Participant writes own outline, then clicks a button to get a one-shot AI-generated draft based on that outline, which populates the revision textbox; participant then revises it.

arms.name: ai revision
arms.description: Participant plans and drafts alone; in revision, three AI tools (argument improver, writing clarity, proof-reader) give 2-4 suggestions each and can auto-implement them; tools can be rerun.

participants.exclusions: 18% of submissions were rejected before analysis, mainly for external AI use or large pastes of outside text, detected by telemetry, manual log inspection, and the Pangram AI detector (pp. 5 and 23, Section 3.4 and Appendix E). An additional two participants were excluded due to data loss (p. 23, Appendix E). The number of submissions before exclusion and the exclusions by arm are not stated. Analyses keep all remaining participants by assigned condition regardless of tool use; a robustness check restricts to active tool users (ai plan 43, ai revision 51; p. 32, Table 8).
participants.who: Prolific workers, desktop users, English-speaking adults aged 22-65, 100% approval rate and at least 100 prior submissions; mean age 38 (SD 10); 99% native English speakers (250/253).
participants.country: United States, United Kingdom, or Australia (split not stated)
participants.quote: Our final data sample consisted of 253 participants distributed almost evenly across the four study conditions ( no ai : n=60; ai plan : n=66; ai draft : n=66; ai revision : n=61).

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI gpt-4.1-mini, accessed August 2025 (p. 5, Section 3.3). Appendix F.2 (p. 24) instead calls the support model 'GPT-4o', an inconsistency in the document. Essay grader: OpenAI o4-mini.
ai_tool.how_used: Role differs by arm: ai plan = ideas_supplied (on-request thesis statements and outlines); ai draft = AI writes a full draft from the participant's outline (one-shot, no regeneration); ai revision = refinement (suggestions on the participant's own draft with optional auto-implementation). No free chat. Use was optional in ai plan (65% requested ideas) and ai revision (84% ran a tool) (p. 8; p. 31, Table 7).

task.description: 200-300 word argumentative essay on a chosen TOEFL/IELTS-style policy question (e.g., banning smartphones in schools), written in three stages: outline, draft, revision.
task.duration: Planning max 10 min (min 60 words), drafting max 15 min (min 300 words), revision max 10 min (min 250 words); paid for an estimated 40-minute session (pp. 4-5).

outcomes.name: Essay quality (quality_overall), mean of three IELTS-based subscores
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 0-9 composite = mean of (i) quality of argument, (ii) coherence and cohesion, (iii) lexical resource and grammar, adapted from IELTS Writing Task 2 band descriptors. Graded by o4-mini (high reasoning effort) with the rubric and 30 teacher-graded essays as few-shot examples; validated against 20 held-out teacher-graded essays, tolerance-based Cohen's kappa = 0.85 (pp. 6-7, Section 4.1; pp. 24-25, Appendix F). This is a writing-quality rubric, not a creativity rating. Model controls for prompt fixed effects, final word count, and total minutes on task, with heteroskedasticity-robust SEs (p. 28, H.4). Robustness: active tool users only (p. 32, Table 8). Subscores are not reported separately.

outcomes.name: Word count of final essay
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of words in the final submitted essay, reported as editing telemetry (mean, SD by condition). Not a creativity measure and not analyzed with a test; it is used as a covariate in the quality model (p. 7, Section 4.2).

Word count mean (SD): ai-plan 341 (106) vs no-ai 344 (96); arm ns 66 and 60. No test reported.
Word count mean (SD): ai-revision 387 (94) vs no-ai 344 (96); arm ns 61 and 60. No test reported; text calls it 'higher word count' (p. 8, Section 5.1).

company_involvement.description: No company author, funder, or data partner is stated. OpenAI models were used as tools and Pangram as an AI detector.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1 affiliations; p. 5, Section 3.3; p. 23, Appendix E

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 met: individuals were randomly assigned to no AI or one of three generative-AI conditions (p. 4, Section 3.3). Criterion 2 met: 253 people analyzed (p. 5, Section 3.4). Criterion 3 not met: the task is an argumentative essay, and the only outcome scored on the output is writing quality on an IELTS proficiency rubric (argument quality, coherence, lexical resource and grammar), not creativity, novelty, or diversity across people (pp. 6-7, Section 4.1; p. 24, Appendix F). The headline outcomes (ownership, attribution of ideas and text) are self-reports. N-gram retention (p. 8, Table 2) compares one person's own texts across stages, not different people's outputs. Borderline only if Review 1 counts IELTS 'quality of argument' as usefulness on a creative task.

one_line_finding: Among 253 Prolific writers, an AI-generated draft raised IELTS-rubric essay quality (adjusted mean 7.27 vs 5.69 with no AI; C2 +1.45 [1.14, 1.77] over the other AI arms), while AI planning (5.85) and revision support (5.79) were similar to no AI (p. 29, Table 6c; p. 11, Figure 6b); the paper measures writing quality and self-reported ownership, not creativity.
open_questions: Whether an argumentative essay graded on an IELTS writing-quality rubric counts as a creative task with a 'usefulness' outcome under the codebook. This form says no.
The support model is named gpt-4.1-mini on p. 5 but GPT-4o on pp. 6 and 24; the document is inconsistent.
Number of submissions before the 18% exclusion, and exclusions by arm, are not stated, so n_randomized is unknown.
notes: Version on file is arXiv v2 (11 Jun 2026) in DIS '26 format; the candidate record lists the DIS 2026 proceedings DOI. Outcomes not listed because they are self-reported: ownership (own_primary, 1-7; Table 6a, p. 29), control/agency items, effort, and ideas/text attributed to AI (Table 6b, p. 29). Process telemetry not listed: keystrokes, time, backspace %, paste events (Table 1, p. 8), within-person k-gram retention across stages (Table 2, p. 8), and AI engagement (Table 7, p. 31). The paper reports no diversity or homogenization measure across participants. No standard deviations are printed for essay quality; Figure 11c (p. 30) shows its distribution by condition as box plots. A $5 bonus went to the top 5% of essays by quality score (p. 5).
